target.title: FastLTS: Non-Autoregressive End-to-End Unconstrained Lip-to-Speech Synthesis
target.venue: Proceedings of the 30th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM ’22), October 10–14, 2022, Lisbon, Portugal

read.pdf: Fig. 1–6 and Tables 1–6 read from the supplied full text

entries.text: FastLTS is presented as a non-autoregressive end-to-end system that directly generates speech audio from unconstrained talking videos with low latency and a relatively small model.
entries.condition: Authors' claimed use-time behavior; silent talking-face video input, direct waveform output.
entries.quote: we propose FastLTS, a non-autoregressive end-to-end model which can directly synthesize high-quality speech audios from unconstrained talking videos with low latency

entries.text: Novelty claim: to the authors' knowledge, this is the first practical transformer-based visual frontend for lip-to-speech synthesis and lipreading.
entries.condition: Qualified by 'as far as we know'; component is the visual frontend, not a claim that transformers are new generally.
entries.quote: As far as we know, this is the first practical transformer-based visual frontend for lip-to-speech synthesis and lipreading.

entries.text: Mel-spectrogram generation speedup over the autoregressive Lip2Wav model at the configured input length.
entries.condition: 3-second input sequence; comparison with Lip2Wav; speed experiment uses Chemistry Lectures speaker, batch size 1, Intel-Xeon E5-2678 CPU and NVIDIA RTX-2080Ti GPU.
entries.quote: We can see that the acceleration ratio reaches 9.14× when the input length is 3 seconds which is the configured input length in FastLTS and Lip2Wav.

entries.text: Waveform generation speedup over the autoregressive Lip2Wav model at the configured input length.
entries.condition: 3-second input sequence; comparison with Lip2Wav; Chemistry Lectures speaker, batch size 1, Intel-Xeon E5-2678 CPU and NVIDIA RTX-2080Ti GPU.
entries.quote:
The acceleration ratio of wave-
form synthesis reaches 19.76× when the input length is 3 seconds.

entries.text: Lip2Wav corpus description: real-world lecture videos from five speakers, about 20 hours per speaker, with vocabulary exceeding 5,000 words per speaker.
entries.condition: Corpus-level description; FastLTS experiments use only the three speakers listed in t6.

entries.text: Lip2Wav experiments use Chess Analysis, Chemistry Lectures, and Hardware Security, at 30 fps with audio sampled at 16 kHz; training/evaluation splits are said to match Lip2Wav [24].
entries.condition: Lip2Wav dataset, named speakers; paper does not reproduce [24]'s partition details.
entries.quote: We conduct our experiments on 3 speakers, which are Chess Analysis, Chemistry Lectures and Hardware Security.

entries.text: GRID corpus description: 34 speakers, 1,000 sentences per speaker, a 51-word vocabulary, restricted grammar, and 6–10 words per sentence.
entries.condition: Corpus-level description of the constrained GRID benchmark.

entries.text: GRID experiments are conducted on three speakers; their identities and separate per-speaker results are not given in the text.
entries.condition: GRID; paper describes the subset count, not the selected identities.
entries.quote: We conduct our experiments on three speakers in the GRID dataset to prove the adaptability on small constrained datasets of our model.

entries.text: Training examples are contiguous 3-second clips; audio is sampled at 16 kHz and converted to 80-bin mel spectrograms with window size 800 and hop size 200.
entries.unit: seconds; samples/s; samples; samples; mel bins
entries.condition: Preprocessing for audio/video training examples; the paper does not state waveform loudness normalization.

entries.text: Faces are detected with S3FD, cropped, and resized to 96×96 pixels.
entries.condition: Visual preprocessing; crop/face detector S3FD; training and evaluation images.

entries.text: GRID-only augmentation flips facial images horizontally with probability 40% and randomly crops 0–7.2% of horizontal or vertical pixels with probability 40%.
entries.condition: GRID training data only; intended to improve performance and avoid overfitting.

entries.text: Visual frontend factorizes processing into spatial and temporal transformer stages, with a 3D-convolutional tokenization layer and Performer-style linear-approximated spatial attention.
entries.condition: Visual encoding of video frames; spatial attention is restricted to tokens from the same temporal index, followed by temporal modeling.
entries.quote:
It consists of a 3D-
convolutional layer, a layer normalization layer and a max-pooling
layer.

entries.text: Tokenization uses a 5×5×5 3D-convolution kernel and token dimension 32; spatial transformer has four layers, hidden dimension 36, and six heads.
entries.unit: kernel dimensions; token dimension; layers; hidden dimension; heads
entries.condition: Visual encoder model configuration.

entries.text: Temporal transformer has four layers and eight heads; hidden dimension is 384 for Lip2Wav and 160 for GRID, with feed-forward output dimension four times the temporal hidden dimension.
entries.condition: Dataset-specific visual encoder configuration; acoustic conditional module uses the temporal transformer's hidden size and number of layers.

entries.text: Visual features are duplicated to align with acoustic frames at factor audio-feature frames per second divided by video fps; at 80 acoustic frames/s and 30 video fps the repeating factors are 3,3,2.
entries.unit: acoustic frames/s ÷ video frames/s; duplication factors
entries.condition: Temporal alignment before the acoustic conditional module; factors distribute non-integer alignment across frames.

entries.text: The acoustic conditional module is a non-autoregressive decoder that maps visual features to acoustic features; its auxiliary mel output is only a training aid and is not fed to the waveform generator.
entries.condition: Inference waveform path bypasses the auxiliary mel output.
entries.quote: Note that this module does not feed mel-spectrograms into the waveform generator, and the auxiliary mel layer is only used to assist training.

entries.text: The final audio output is synthesized directly by a HiFi-GAN-structure waveform generator from projected acoustic features.
entries.condition: The projected acoustic features have the same dimensionality as the auxiliary mel layer (80); the mel representation is not an inference-stage intermediary.
entries.quote: We then feed the projected features to the generator to synthesize audio waveform.

entries.text: Two-stage training stage 1 excludes the waveform generator and trains visual encoder plus acoustic conditional module against auxiliary mel spectrograms using SSIM and L1 losses.
entries.condition: Stage 1 uses paired video and ground-truth audio-derived mel spectrograms; SSIM/L1 loss weights are not numerically reported.

entries.text: Stage 2 removes the auxiliary mel output and trains the waveform generator with adversarial, mel-spectrogram, and feature-matching losses; for the large unconstrained set, visual encoder and acoustic module are frozen.
entries.condition: Large Lip2Wav training; multi-period and multi-scale discriminators; only waveform-generator parameters optimized in stage 2.
entries.quote:
Therefore, we freeze the parame-
ters of the visual encoder and the acoustic conditional module in
the second stage and only optimize the parameters of the waveform
generator.

entries.text: Authors report that training the waveform generator on sampled windows lowers computation/memory while retaining performance on small data, but shrinks context and damages visual encoding on large unconstrained data, motivating freezing upstream modules.
entries.condition: Wave-generator training window; caveat is specifically the large unconstrained dataset versus small dataset behavior.
entries.quote:
How-
ever, for large unconstrained dataset, training the whole model in
this way will damage the encoding ability of the visual encoder due
to the shrink of context window.

entries.text: The waveform-generator sampling window is 1.2 seconds; the two stages use Adam and AdamW with initial learning rates 2×10⁻³ and 2×10⁻⁴ respectively.
entries.condition: Training configuration; optimizer order follows the paper's stated stage order.

entries.text: Subjective evaluation uses Amazon Mechanical Turk, three 1–5 Likert scales (quality, intelligibility, naturalness), over 300 respondents per test item, and reports MOS; respondents were paid about $7.2/hour.
entries.condition: Generated and ground-truth audio; Lip2Wav and GRID MOS. Exact item selection, rater exclusions, and aggregation procedure are not specified.
entries.quote: We paid the respondents around $7.2 hourly.

questions.q: What does ‘end-to-end’ mean operationally, given the training procedure?
questions.answer: At inference, the model generates the waveform directly and does not pass an auxiliary mel spectrogram into the generator; training nevertheless uses two stages, with a mel-supervised first stage.

questions.q: How strong is the evidence for audio-quality superiority across benchmarks?
questions.answer: Lip2Wav MOS improves on most reported dimensions and speakers, while Chemistry Lectures intelligibility is lower than Lip2Wav; GRID MOS beats Lip2Wav but is below ground truth, and FastLTS PESQ trails VCA-GAN.

questions.q: How comparable and reproducible are the benchmark comparisons?
questions.answer: The paper inherits Lip2Wav splits by reference and leaves speaker overlap, validation/model selection, random seeds, MOS item selection, and PESQ cross-paper protocol matching unresolved; no code URL is linked in the paper.

questions.q: How far does the evaluation support generalization beyond the tested speakers and recording conditions?
questions.answer: The reported experiments use three named Lip2Wav speakers and three unspecified GRID speakers; the authors explicitly leave multi-speaker extension and low-resolution video to future work.

questions.q: What deployment trade-off is quantified, and what remains unmeasured?
questions.answer: The paper reports parameter counts and speedups under a specified single-GPU, batch-one setup, but does not define parameter-count boundaries or provide a detailed timing protocol or measured peak memory.
